planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright indirect to low light in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; move outdoors only after nights stay reliably above 60°F and bring back in well before fall frost.

directions: Grow in bright indirect to low light in moist, humus-rich, well-drained potting mix, shielding the plant from any direct sun that can scorch its thin leaves. Vittata produces elongated, elliptical leaves in medium green boldly marked with fine, pale cream to white pinstripes running parallel to the lateral veins, a more linear, feathery pattern than the broad blotches of many other calatheas, and like its relatives the leaves fold upward at night. Native to the understory of Amazonian rainforest in Venezuela, Guyana, and Suriname, it is a slow grower that rewards patience with a tidy, upright rosette well suited to tabletop display. Maintain high humidity and consistently moist, never soggy soil, use filtered or rain water where possible, and increase humidity around the plant to prevent the crisp brown leaf edges that dry indoor air can cause.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Calathea and Goeppertia Species for Florida

common_name: Schumi Red Peperomia (Deep Red Ripple Peperomia)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky potting mix; Schumi Red stores water in its thick leaves and stems and prefers to dry out somewhat between waterings.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky potting mix, allowing the top inch or two to dry before watering again. Schumi Red bears small, rounded, deeply corrugated leaves in a rich, near-solid reddish-purple that deepens further on the leaf underside, a more uniformly dark, rippled look than the pointed, bicolor leaves of other red-leaved caperata selections. Its compact, mounding habit and slow growth make it a good fit for a windowsill, dish garden, or terrarium where space is limited. Keep it away from direct midday sun, which can wash out the color, and propagate by leaf or stem cuttings rooted in moist, well-drained mix.

common_name: Clevelandii Peace Lily (Classic Heirloom Peace Lily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in deep to moderate shade; Clevelandii is one of the oldest peace lily selections still grown and a mid-sized, reliable classic houseplant form.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in deep to moderate shade, keeping the plant warm above 60°F and away from direct sun and cold drafts. Clevelandii is a long-cultivated, mid-sized peace lily with glossy, dark green, lance-shaped leaves and the classic white spathes of the genus, grown commercially for decades before larger modern hybrids became more common in the trade. It tolerates low indoor light and irregular watering better than most houseplants, drooping dramatically when thirsty but reviving quickly once watered, and it reblooms intermittently through the year given adequate warmth and humidity. Divide congested clumps at repotting time to produce new plants, and keep it out of reach of pets since all parts are toxic if chewed or ingested.

common_name: Variegata Peace Lily (White-Streaked Compact Peace Lily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained soil in medium to low light; Variegata stays more compact than plain Spathiphyllum wallisii and needs slightly brighter indirect light to hold its white leaf streaking.

directions: Grow in medium to low indirect light in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil, giving it slightly brighter conditions than a plain green peace lily to help preserve its variegation. This compact selection of Spathiphyllum wallisii produces long, lance-shaped leaves irregularly streaked and splashed with creamy white over green, smaller in stature than most peace lily cultivars and well suited to a tabletop or terrarium setting. Variegation can fade toward solid green in very low light or on vigorous new growth, so rotate the plant for even light exposure and remove any leaves that revert fully to green if a strongly patterned specimen is the goal. Keep soil evenly moist but not waterlogged and maintain good humidity, since this cultivar is somewhat less vigorous and less drought-tolerant than its all-green parent.

common_name: Power Petite Peace Lily (Dwarf Dark-Leaf Peace Lily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained soil in medium to low light; Power Petite is one of the smallest commercially available peace lily selections, well suited to small pots, desks, and tabletops.

directions: Grow in medium to low indirect light in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil, keeping it warm and away from cold drafts and direct sun. Power Petite is a diminutive peace lily with small, glossy, dark green leaves in a dense clumping habit and proportionally small white spathes, staying far more compact at maturity than common peace lily selections and better suited to a small pot on a desk or shelf than a floor planter. Like other peace lilies it tolerates low indoor light and occasional missed waterings, wilting visibly when thirsty but recovering quickly once watered. Divide the clump when repotting to produce new plants, and keep it away from pets, since all parts are toxic if chewed.

common_name: Starlight Peace Lily (Free-Flowering Wavy-Leaf Peace Lily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained soil in medium to bright indirect light; Starlight is a compact, heavy-blooming peace lily selected for producing an unusually large number of flowers per plant.

directions: Grow in medium to bright indirect light in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil, keeping the plant warm and sheltered from direct sun. Starlight forms a compact, free-branching clump of narrow, dark green, waxy leaves with gently wavy margins, and is notable for producing unusually heavy flushes of pointed white spathes well above the foliage, often blooming for much of the year under good indoor conditions. Its tidy, floriferous habit makes it a popular choice for interior plantscaping and gift plants where abundant bloom matters as much as foliage. Water when the surface of the soil begins to dry, and expect the leaves to droop visibly as a reliable thirst signal before they suffer lasting damage.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a well-draining potting mix; Minima is a dwarf, more compact form of the aluminum plant well suited to small pots, dish gardens, and terrariums.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in a well-draining, peat-based potting mix, keeping humidity moderate to high for the fullest, most compact growth. Minima is a dwarf selection of the aluminum plant, staying noticeably smaller than the standard form while keeping its glossy, quilted green leaves raised in silvery, metallic blotches between the veins. Its naturally bushy, low habit suits a small pot, terrarium, or dish garden better than the larger standard aluminum plant, which can become leggy over time. Pinch growing tips regularly to keep the plant dense, and take stem cuttings to propagate, since Pilea cadierei tends to lose vigor and become sparse with age.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Pilea cadierei

common_name: Silver Band Prayer Plant (Wide Silver-Midrib Maranta)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained potting mix; Silver Band wants high humidity and consistent moisture and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained potting mix, favoring a spot with high ambient humidity. Silver Band carries a broad, pale silvery-green stripe running the length of each matte green leaf, flanked by neatly symmetrical veins, a cleaner and more minimal pattern than the boldly blotched or red-veined Maranta cultivars. Like all prayer plants its leaves fold upward at night and flatten again each morning, a daily movement that is part of its appeal as a houseplant. Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged, mist regularly or run a humidifier to prevent crisp brown leaf edges in dry indoor air, and divide congested clumps in spring to propagate and renew the plant's vigor.

planting.note: Divide offsets from the base in spring or early summer when repotting into fresh, well-drained mix; Christina tolerates fairly low indoor light but grows more densely in bright, indirect exposure.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect to low light in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, keeping the plant above 60°F and out of direct sun. Christina forms a neat, slow-growing clump of broad, sword-shaped leaves in pale silvery-green with darker green margins and central splashes, a quieter, more understated pattern than the brighter pink- or red-blushed Aglaonema hybrids. Its compact, tidy habit and tolerance of dim interiors make it a dependable choice for offices and low-light rooms where few other flowering-category plants perform well. Allow the top inch or two of potting mix to dry between waterings, mist occasionally to discourage spider mites, and divide the clump at the base to propagate new plants.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Aglaonema production guide

planting.note: Divide offsets from the base in spring or early summer when repotting into fresh, well-drained mix; Stripes tolerates low to medium indoor light, including dim, north-facing rooms.

directions: Grow in low to medium indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, keeping the plant warm and away from direct sun that can scorch the leaves. Stripes carries large, ovate, lime-green leaves marked with narrow, silvery-white bands that arch outward from the centerline toward the leaf margins, a bold, symmetrical pattern that reads well even in dim corners. It is among the more shade-tolerant Aglaonema hybrids available, holding its color and habit with minimal light while still growing steadily. Water when the top few inches of potting mix have dried, keep temperatures above 60°F, and divide the clump at repotting time to produce new plants.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Aglaonema production guide

common_name: Emerald Star Chinese Evergreen (Dark Green Speckled Aglaonema)

planting.note: Divide offsets from the base in spring or early summer when repotting into fresh, well-drained mix; Emerald Star is a dense, upright, vigorous grower that tolerates fairly low indoor light.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect to low light in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, keeping the plant warm and sheltered from direct sun. Emerald Star forms a dense, upright, outward-spreading clump of dark green leaves flecked with white, light green, and dark green spots and speckles around a pale midrib, giving the foliage a busy, finely mottled texture distinct from the broader-blotched Aglaonema hybrids. Its vigorous, full growth habit fills a container quickly compared with slower-growing Aglaonema cultivars, while still adapting to low light with somewhat slower growth. Allow the top inch or two of potting mix to dry between waterings and divide the clump at the base to propagate new plants.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Aglaonema production guide

common_name: Black Mamba Rex Begonia (Large Near-Black Star-Leaf Rex Begonia)

planting.note: Grow year-round as a houseplant or shaded patio container plant in bright, indirect light; move outdoors to a shaded spot for summer only after night temperatures stay reliably above 50°F.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, keeping soil evenly moist but never waterlogged to avoid rhizome rot. Black Mamba produces large, star-shaped leaves in a deep, near-black green that darken further with maturity, among the largest and darkest leaves of any widely grown Rex begonia, with occasional pink winter flowers providing soft contrast against the foliage. Its bold scale and dramatic coloring make a single specimen a strong focal point in a mixed shade container or windowsill grouping. Provide higher humidity than typical houseplants prefer, water only when the surface of the mix begins to dry, and divide the rhizome at repotting time to produce new plants.

common_name: Tornado Rex Begonia (Spiral-Centered Black Speckled Rex Begonia)

planting.note: Grow year-round as a houseplant or shaded patio container plant in bright, indirect light; move outdoors to a shaded spot for summer only after night temperatures stay reliably above 50°F.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, keeping soil evenly moist but never soggy to avoid rhizome rot. Tornado bears large, heart-shaped, velvety black leaves scattered with pink and white speckles and blotches, with a tightly coiled spiral at the leaf center where the petiole attaches, a whorled growth pattern shared by several Rex begonia cultivars but especially pronounced here. The dramatic, dark backdrop makes the pink speckling pop and gives the plant strong textural interest even without flowers. Provide higher humidity than typical houseplants prefer, water only when the surface of the mix begins to dry, and divide the rhizome at repotting time to produce new plants.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in a hanging basket or on a shelf edge in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky potting mix, letting the mix dry somewhat between waterings.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky potting mix in a hanging basket or elevated shelf position that lets its stems trail freely. Pepperspot produces a dense cascade of small, round, glossy green leaves set against contrasting reddish stems, a fine-textured, fast-growing trailer useful for softening the edge of a plant shelf or mixed container. Like other peperomias it stores water in its leaves and stems and tolerates drying out between waterings better than most tropical foliage plants, making it forgiving of occasional neglect. Pinch growing tips to encourage fuller, bushier growth and propagate easily from stem cuttings rooted in moist potting mix.
